q: A company trains a résumé-screening model on ten years of past hiring decisions, when most people hired were men. The model now ranks equally qualified women lower. What is the main problem?
opts: A fairness problem caused by bias in the training data
A privacy breach of the applicants' data
A reliability problem caused by slow hardware
A transparency feature working as designed
exp: A model learns patterns from its training data, so if past decisions were biased, the model repeats that bias and treats equally qualified groups differently, which breaks the fairness principle. Nothing here exposes personal data, so it is not a privacy breach. Hardware speed has nothing to do with the ranking, and transparency is about explaining the system, not about the unequal outcome.

q: An AI system that approves refunds makes a harmful decision. According to the accountability principle, who is responsible?
opts: The people and organization behind the system
Only the customer who asked for the refund in the first place
Nobody, because the decision was automated by software
exp: Accountability means that the people who design, build and deploy an AI system remain answerable for how it operates and for its impact. A model cannot be held responsible, and responsibility does not move to the customer or disappear just because a decision was automated. Organizations show accountability through governance, named owners, reviews and ways to correct mistakes.

q: A voice assistant was designed and tested only with young native speakers. The team now involves older users, people with speech impairments and people with different accents in design reviews and testing. Which principle are they applying?
exp: Inclusiveness asks teams to design AI that empowers everyone, and a key practice is involving people with a wide range of abilities and backgrounds in design and testing. Accountability is about governance and ownership, privacy and security is about protecting data, and transparency is about helping people understand the system, so none of them describe bringing more diverse users into the design process.

q: Images created with image-generation models in Microsoft Foundry carry Content Credentials that show they were generated by AI. Which responsible AI principle does this mainly support?
exp: Content Credentials add provenance information to generated images so people can see that AI created them. Disclosing that content is AI-generated is transparency, because people understand what they are looking at. Reliability and safety is about safe and consistent behavior, fairness is about equal treatment, and accountability is about who is answerable for the system, so they are not the main purpose of the label.

q: For each of the following statements about privacy and security, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Keeping chat logs indefinitely by default is a recommended privacy practice.
Prompts and completions sent to Azure OpenAI models in Microsoft Foundry are used to train OpenAI's public models.
Limiting access to an AI app's data with role-based access control supports the privacy and security principle.
exp: No for the first: privacy practice is to keep personal data only as long as needed, so storing every log forever by default increases risk. No for the second: Microsoft states that customer prompts and completions are not used to train OpenAI models and are not available to OpenAI. Yes for the third: role-based access control makes sure only approved identities can reach the data, which protects it.

q: Which THREE practices support reliability and safety before and after a generative AI chatbot is released? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: Turn off all logging so that nothing can be reviewed
Plan a fallback, such as handing the user over to a person
Red-team the chatbot with adversarial and harmful prompts
Evaluate responses on a test dataset and keep monitoring after release
exp: Red teaming finds weaknesses before release, evaluation and monitoring show how the chatbot behaves over time, and a fallback limits harm when it cannot answer safely. Without logs problems cannot be investigated, and the highest temperature makes answers less predictable.

q: Match each description to Microsoft's responsible AI principle. Each principle is used once.
items: AI systems should treat all people fairly
AI systems should perform reliably and safely
AI systems should be secure and respect privacy
AI systems should empower everyone and engage people
People should be accountable for AI systems
exp: These six statements are the short definitions Microsoft uses for its responsible AI principles: fair treatment is fairness, reliable and safe performance is reliability and safety, secure and private is privacy and security, empowering everyone is inclusiveness, being understandable is transparency, and people being answerable is accountability. Knowing the one-line definition of each principle helps with scenario questions.

q: A skin-condition model is 95% accurate overall, but only 70% accurate for people with darker skin tones. What should the team do next?
opts: Release the model now, because the overall accuracy is already high
Raise the decision threshold for all users to reduce false alarms
Remove skin color from the images
Measure each group separately and improve the training data for weak groups
exp: An overall score can hide much worse results for some groups. Measuring metrics per group, often called disaggregated evaluation, shows the gap, and adding representative data for under-served groups helps close it, which supports fairness. Releasing based only on the average ignores the harm. Changing one threshold for everyone does not fix the gap, and color cannot simply be removed from medical images.

q: Complete the sentence by selecting the correct option for each blank.
tpl: Microsoft's responsible AI principles are fairness, reliability and safety, {0}, inclusiveness, transparency, and {1}.
exp: Microsoft's six responsible AI principles are fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability. Speed, profitability, scalability and availability can be business or technical goals, but they are not responsible AI principles. Remembering the full list of six makes it easier to recognize which principle a scenario describes.

q: A hospital builds an AI assistant that suggests how urgently patients should be seen. Which design best supports reliability and safety?
opts: Let the model act on its suggestions without review when staff are too busy
Have a qualified clinician review each suggestion before it is acted on
Hide the model's confidence from staff
Disable the content filters so that staff get faster answers in emergencies
exp: In high-impact scenarios a human in the loop who reviews AI suggestions before action reduces the chance of harm when the model is wrong, which supports reliability and safety. Acting without review removes that safeguard. Hiding confidence information takes away a signal that helps people judge the output. Disabling content filters weakens safety and does not make suggestions more reliable.

q: What is a large language model (LLM)?
opts: A database of prepared answers that is searched each time a user asks a question
A rules engine in which developers program by hand how to answer each question
A model trained on large amounts of text to understand and generate language
A spreadsheet macro that formats text
exp: A large language model is a neural network, usually based on the transformer architecture, trained on very large text collections so that it can understand and generate natural language for tasks such as answering questions, summarizing and writing. It does not store prepared answers, it is not a hand-written rules engine, and it is not a formatting macro.

q: In a generative AI solution, what is a prompt?
opts: The input that you send to the model
The data the model was trained on before release
The name of the model deployment that you call
The monthly bill for using the model in your app
exp: A prompt is the input you give a generative model, such as a question, an instruction, examples or extra context, and the model generates a response from it. Training data is what the model learned from before it was deployed. The deployment name identifies the model endpoint, and the bill is unrelated to how the model is used in a request.

q: Which statement describes an advantage of a small language model, such as a Phi model, compared with a large language model?
opts: It always gives more accurate answers than a large model on every task
It has an unlimited context window
It cannot be fine-tuned, so its behavior never changes over time
It needs less compute, so it can cost less and run on smaller local devices
exp: Small language models have fewer parameters, so they need less memory and compute, respond faster and can run at lower cost or even on devices, while handling many focused tasks well. They are not more accurate on every task; large models are usually stronger at broad or complex reasoning. No model has an unlimited context window, and small models can be fine-tuned.

q: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Setting the temperature close to 0 makes a model's output more predictable.
By default, a generative model searches the internet before it answers.
A model only knows facts up to its training cutoff unless your app gives it more current information.
exp: Yes for the first: a low temperature makes the model choose the most likely tokens, so answers vary less. No for the second: a model generates text from what it learned and does not browse the web unless the solution adds a tool such as web grounding. Yes for the third: a model learns from data collected before its training cutoff, so newer facts must be supplied, for example through retrieval or a search tool.

q: Which approach most reduces the chance that a chat solution invents facts about a company's products?
opts: Ground each prompt with trusted product data
Increase the temperature so that answers vary more
Send shorter prompts that contain no extra product context
exp: Grounding gives the model trusted, relevant content to answer from, and asking for citations makes it easier to check that answers come from that content, which reduces made-up facts. A higher temperature adds randomness and can increase invented details. Removing context or the system message takes away information and guidance, which makes unsupported answers more likely.

q: GPT models are generative pre-trained transformers. Which part of the transformer architecture do they use to generate text one token at a time?
exp: GPT models are decoder-based transformers: the decoder uses attention over the tokens so far to predict the next token, which is how text is generated step by step. Encoder-only models, such as BERT, are mainly used to understand and represent text rather than to generate it. Convolutional networks are typical for images, and decision trees are a different kind of machine learning model.

q: Match each description to the technique it describes. Each technique can be used once or not at all.
items: Adding passages found in your documents to the prompt
Further training a model on many example inputs and outputs
Including a few worked examples of the task in the prompt
Writing instructions that set the model's role and rules
exp: Retrieval augmented generation adds retrieved content to the prompt so the model answers from your data. Fine-tuning continues training on many examples and changes the model's behavior. Few-shot prompting puts a handful of examples inside the prompt. A system message sets the role and rules. Tokenization only splits text into tokens and does not change how the model answers.

q: Which THREE statements about tokens are correct? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: Model usage and cost are usually measured in tokens
A token is always exactly one complete word
A model's context window is measured in tokens
Tokens are used only for image models
A token can be a part of a word
exp: Usage and cost are usually counted in tokens, the context window is a number of tokens, and tokenizers split many words into pieces, so a token can be a part of a word. A token is therefore not always a whole word, and tokens are used by language models, not only by image models.

q: Complete the sentences by selecting the correct option for each blank.
tpl: Generative AI creates {0} content based on patterns that it learned from its training data. A response that sounds right but is not supported by facts is called {1}.
exp: Generative AI produces new content, such as text, images or code, by using patterns learned during training rather than copying stored content. A fluent answer that is not grounded in facts is called a hallucination. A token is a unit of text and an embedding is a numeric vector, so neither describes an incorrect answer.

q: Put the steps of a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) request in the correct order. Not every step is used.
items: Search an index for passages that match the question
Send the prompt with the retrieved passages to the model
Return the grounded answer, ideally with citations
Fine-tune the model on the question
exp: A RAG request starts with the user's question, then searches an index, often with embeddings, for relevant passages, then sends the question together with those passages to the model, and finally returns an answer grounded in the passages, ideally with citations. Fine-tuning is a separate training process and is not part of answering a single question.

q: You need a model from the Foundry model catalog that turns recorded speech into text. Which model fits?
exp: whisper is a speech-to-text model that transcribes audio, and it can also translate speech to English. gpt-image-1 generates images, text-embedding-3-small creates embedding vectors for search, and Phi-4 is a small language model that works with text, so none of them transcribe audio.

q: Before you deploy a model, where can you read about its capabilities, intended uses, limitations and license?
opts: The model card in the catalog
exp: Each model in the Foundry model catalog has a model card that describes what the model does, how it was trained, its intended uses and limitations, and its license terms. Azure Advisor gives general best-practice tips, the activity log records management operations, and the pricing calculator estimates cost; none of them describe a model's capabilities.

q: A finance team needs a model for complex multi-step calculations and planning, where accuracy matters more than speed. Which type of model should they choose?
exp: Reasoning models work through a problem internally before they answer, which improves results on complex math, logic and planning tasks at the cost of more time and tokens. A small fast model is better for simple, quick answers. Embedding models return vectors and speech synthesis models create audio, so neither solves multi-step problems.

q: Your prompt template ends each answer with the marker ###. You want the model to stop generating as soon as it writes this marker. Which setting should you use?
exp: A stop sequence tells the model to stop generating when it produces a given string, such as ###, and the string itself is not included in the output. Temperature and top P control how random the token choices are, and presence penalty encourages the model to introduce new topics; none of them end the output at a marker.

q: A model keeps repeating the same words and phrases in long answers. Which parameter should you increase?
exp: Frequency penalty lowers the chance of tokens that have already appeared often in the output, so the model repeats itself less. More response tokens allows longer answers but does not reduce repetition, stop sequences only end the output at a marker, and quota controls how much traffic the deployment can handle.

q: For each of the following statements about deployments, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Provisioned deployments are billed only for the tokens that you actually use.
A Global Standard deployment can process requests in any Azure region.
A deployment's tokens-per-minute quota limits how much traffic it can handle.
exp: No for the first: provisioned deployments reserve capacity in provisioned throughput units, which you pay for whether or not you use them; pay-per-token billing applies to standard deployments. Yes for the second: Global Standard routes traffic across Azure's global infrastructure, so processing can happen in any region. Yes for the third: when requests exceed the tokens-per-minute limit, extra calls are rejected with 429 errors.

q: You must choose a model for a support chatbot that serves customers in five languages and lets them upload photos of damaged products. Which TWO criteria matter most? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opts: The model has the longest name in the catalog
The model was the first one released
The model performs well in the languages that the customers use
The model uses the most GPUs
exp: The scenario needs a multimodal model that accepts images and that performs well in all five languages, so those are the deciding capabilities, which you can check in model cards and with your own tests. A model's name, release order and hardware use say nothing about whether it fits the task.

q: Match each description to the deployment type. Each type can be used once or not at all.
items: Asynchronous bulk jobs with a 24-hour target turnaround at a lower price
Reserved processing capacity for steady traffic and predictable latency
Pay per token, and requests can be processed in any Azure region
Pay per token, and processing stays inside a data zone, such as the EU or US
exp: Global Batch runs large asynchronous jobs within a 24-hour target at a discount. Provisioned deployments reserve throughput for predictable performance. Global Standard is pay-per-token with global routing. Data Zone Standard is pay-per-token while keeping processing inside a data zone such as the EU. Standard is a pay-per-token deployment that keeps processing within one Azure geography, which does not match any description here.

q: Complete the sentences by selecting the correct option for each blank.
tpl: To limit how long a response can be, set {0}. To make the model repeat the same words less often, increase {1}.
exp: Max tokens caps the number of tokens the model can generate, so it limits response length. Frequency penalty reduces the likelihood of tokens that have already appeared often, so repetition drops. Temperature and top P control randomness, and stop sequences end output at a given string, so they do not do either job directly.

q: A team wants to try a model quickly with low traffic and no upfront commitment. Later, production will have steady high traffic that needs guaranteed capacity. What should they do?
opts: Use provisioned throughput for development and Global Batch for production
Global Standard first, then provisioned throughput
Use Global Batch for both development and production
Use no deployment and call the model catalog directly
exp: Global Standard is pay-per-token with no commitment, which suits experimentation, while provisioned throughput reserves capacity for steady, predictable production workloads. Provisioned capacity for development wastes money on idle reserved units, and Global Batch is asynchronous, so it cannot serve live users. Models must be deployed, or used through an instant-access option, before applications can call them; the catalog itself is not an endpoint.
